name: Marjolin ulcer
aliases: malignant transformation of a chronic wound

reference.source: Rook's Dermatology / plastic surgery oncology texts
clinicalPearls: Marjolin ulcer is a malignancy arising within chronically inflamed, scarred or ulcerated skin, most commonly a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma, though basal cell carcinoma, melanoma and sarcoma are also reported
Classic settings include old burn scars, chronic venous or pressure ulcers, and the sinus tracts of chronic osteomyelitis, typically after a long latency of years to decades

Malignant transformation should be suspected when a chronic wound changes, developing everted or rolled margins, exuberant granulation, new nodularity, increased pain, bleeding, malodour or failure to heal despite optimal treatment
Because malignant change may be focal, diagnosis requires multiple deep biopsies taken from the margin and base of the suspicious wound
Squamous cell carcinomas arising in burn scars tend to behave more aggressively, with a higher risk of nodal metastasis than typical sun-related cutaneous carcinoma
Staging includes careful examination of the regional lymph nodes and cross-sectional imaging where deep invasion or metastasis is suspected
Treatment is wide local excision to clear margins with management of regional nodes as indicated and appropriate reconstruction, with radiotherapy or systemic therapy as adjuncts in advanced disease
Long-standing wounds and unstable scars should be kept under surveillance and biopsied promptly if they change, since delayed diagnosis worsens outcome
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic tissue injury with repeated cycles of ulceration and repair creates an environment of persistent inflammation, sustained cellular proliferation and impaired local immune surveillance within scarred, poorly vascularised tissue. Over a prolonged latent period, accumulated genetic damage in chronically regenerating keratinocytes, together with the tumour-permissive inflammatory milieu and relative isolation of the scar from immune effector cells, drives malignant transformation, most often to squamous cell carcinoma. The dense scar may also facilitate invasion once malignancy develops and can contribute to the aggressive behaviour seen in some lesions.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic non-healing venous, arterial, pressure or neuropathic ulcer without malignancy
Chronic osteomyelitis with a discharging sinus
Primary cutaneous squamous or basal cell carcinoma unrelated to a wound
Chronic cutaneous infection, including atypical mycobacterial or deep fungal disease
Other cutaneous malignancy such as melanoma or sarcoma
additionalInvestigations: Multiple deep incisional or wedge biopsies from the ulcer margin and base for histology
Regional lymph node examination and ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration or core biopsy of abnormal nodes
Cross-sectional imaging with CT or MRI to assess local invasion and metastasis
Imaging for underlying osteomyelitis where a sinus is present
Staging investigations as directed by the multidisciplinary team
redFlags: A chronic wound that fails to heal despite optimal care
New nodularity, everted edges, bleeding or rapid change in a long-standing ulcer or scar
A wound arising within an old burn scar or a chronic osteomyelitis sinus
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on tumour type, differentiation, depth of invasion and nodal status; well-differentiated lesions detected early can be cured by excision, but nodal metastasis, notably with burn-scar carcinomas, markedly worsens outcome.
pitfalls: Attributing non-healing solely to the underlying ulcer and delaying biopsy
Taking a single superficial biopsy that misses focal malignancy
Underestimating the aggressiveness of burn-scar carcinomas
Performing an excision with inadequate margins
references: Plastic and reconstructive surgery oncology reference texts
National guidance on the management of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
management: Confirm malignancy with multiple deep biopsies from the margin and base of the wound before definitive treatment
Undertake wide local excision of the tumour, most often a squamous cell carcinoma, with clear margins and appropriate reconstruction
Assess regional lymph nodes and perform node dissection for proven or suspected nodal metastasis, given the aggressive behaviour of burn-scar carcinoma
Give adjuvant radiotherapy for high-risk features, positive margins or nodal disease
Consider amputation for extensive limb tumours or malignant transformation complicating chronic osteomyelitis
Maintain surveillance for local recurrence and metastasis after treatment
Prevent progression by managing chronic non-healing wounds and biopsying long-standing scars or ulcers that change
Direct staging and treatment through an oncology multidisciplinary team spanning plastic surgery, oncology and dermatology
